Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette: Jamal, a 25‑year‑old African American journalist who writes hard‑news stories for a regional paper, first felt the terror of the night he was caught on camera as a police officer brandished a baton at a peaceful protest in downtown Atlanta. The officer’s raised hand, the sudden roar of sirens, and the sharp sting of a baton’s crack against his thigh left a shockwave of panic that he could not shake. He remembered the exact smell of gasoline, the screech of metal, and the echo of his own heartbeat in the air, a sensory memory so vivid it seemed more real than any ordinary recollection. That night, the flash of a siren became a trigger that, years later, sends a shiver down his spine whenever he hears the muted thud of footsteps behind him in a quiet hallway or the faint, familiar rhythm of a certain song that once played at a rally. Those moments of trigger force him to throw on an extra layer of clothing, to tuck his jacket tighter around his shoulders, and to scan the dark corners of the room for an unseen presence, actions that serve to conceal himself from the world. The same triggers make his mind race with the possibility of being followed; he cannot focus on his report because his concentration breaks whenever he hears a single footstep. He avoids unfamiliar places, fearing that an unknown environment could harbor unseen danger, and constantly checks behind him, looking for a shadow that might be an attacker. Even the simple act of turning around to verify there is no one behind him heightens his sense of threat. Because Jamal believes the trauma has robbed him of his former ease and vigor, he has come to see his life as ruined. He thinks he has lost the happiness he once felt, that the event destroyed his sense of purpose, and that he is no longer capable of doing the work that once defined him. Those negative appraisals drive him to keep his clothes concealed, to avoid any memory that might remind him of his loss, and to suppress all emotions, fearing that any positive or negative feeling could be a spark that triggers a flashback. The belief that he is no longer capable keeps him on high alert: every new assignment feels like a threat, and he can barely focus on writing because the world around him feels like a battlefield. His sense of being unable to function feeds the feeling of threat and fuels the memory of the night, which in turn reinforces his negative view of his life. The memory of the baton’s crack and the officer’s shout is the seed from which Jamal’s anxiety grows. It fuels a belief that the world is dangerous, and that danger is omnipresent, so he checks behind him every time he steps into a hallway, even when there is no one present. The act of checking triggers the memory again, and the memory reinforces the feeling that the police’s threat was real and that he cannot escape it. The threat of being pursued makes him pull on his jacket, keep his head down, and avoid leaving the office building, which in turn makes him more cautious of unfamiliar spaces. This caution is a self‑reinforcing cycle: the more he avoids new places, the more he believes the world is dangerous; the more dangerous he thinks the world is, the more he avoids unfamiliar places. Each time he hides under a coat, he feels that he is protecting himself, but that sense of protection only deepens the feeling that he is helpless, a thought that reinforces his negative appraisal that he is no longer capable of doing the work that once mattered. The more he hides, the more he feels trapped, the more he feels his life is destroyed, and the more he feels the memory is a living reality that he cannot shake. When he finally hears footsteps, the memory of the night rushes back, the threat that he cannot be safe rises, and he scrambles to conceal himself, closing the loop that has kept him in a state of hyper‑vigilance for years. After months of feeling a sense of panic that made even the simplest office commute feel like a hostage situation, Jamal’s partner urged him to seek help. He realized he was missing deadlines, his writing had become terse and distracted, and his relationship was strained because he would leave work early and hide in his apartment to escape the world. The most daunting fear that keeps him from leaving his house is that hearing a single footstep or hearing that particular song will bring the image of a baton cracking into his mind again. He hopes that therapy will give him a way to confront these memories so that he no longer feels his life has been destroyed, and so that he can once again step into a newsroom without fearing that every footstep might be the last.
